newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAFRICA RAPPED FOR DRAGGING FEET ON REGIONAL TRADE.
newsitem.headline: SAFRICA RAPPED FOR DRAGGING FEET ON REGIONAL TRADE.

text.p: South Africa was criticised by regional parliamentarians on Friday for appearing to drag its feet on the ratification of a protocol to set up a regional free trade area.

Representatives of 10 of the 12 Southern African Development Community (SADC) states, only two of which have ratified the treaty, were attending the first trade workshop of the SADC Parliamentary Forum.

South Africa Department of Trade and Industry assistant director John Kodisang raised the hackles of several delegates when he said that South Africa wanted more concrete details of what would be involved before it would ratify the protocol, which was approved by regional leaders in September last year.
"There is no way that we are going to sign a blank cheque. There are quite a number of issues that have to be clarified, including rules of origin," he said.
The protocol will only become binding on all member states once it has been ratified by two-thirds of SADC members. From that date, the aim is to phase in a free trade area within eight years.
So far, only Mauritius and Tanzania have ratified the protocol.

Kodisang said that the South African government wanted to consult widely with interested parties, including business and labour, about its initial offer in the negotiations on a free trade area because this could affect the economy as a whole.
"There is no way that South Africa can begin making offers without consulting with the major stakeholders because that is not going to fly at all," he said.
All major economic issues in South Africa are debated by the government-business-labour forum, the National Economic and Development Council (Nedlac), before they are enacted.
Kodisang said that he believed South Africa would be able to consider ratifying the protocol towards the end of the year.
Zimbabwean MP Tirivanha Muduraki congratulated Tanzania and Mauritius for signing up to the agreement.
"They have got visionary leaders who look beyond their African noses. They have set a very good precedent because they have faith in this grouping," he said.
He warned that South Africa should not try to use the excuse of needing to consult interest groups as a delaying tactic.
SADC groups South Africa, Zimbabwe, Zambia, Botswana, Namibia, Malawi, Tanzania, Mauritius, Mozambique, Angola, Lesotho and Swaziland.
